scenes.animation: A colourful wedding family photo. Zippy zooms in with a magnifying glass: a cousin's nose glows and a dotted line links it to Grandpa's nose, while the cousin's brother has a different nose with a question mark over it.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, my cousin has Grandpa's nose, but his own brother doesn't. Who decided that?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Heredity and variation, working together. Heredity passes traits on reliably. Variation makes each child a little different.

scenes.animation: A parent cartoon and offspring cartoon stand side by side with matching body outlines; small differences glow in orange. Labels: 'Heredity = inheritance of traits', 'common body design + subtle differences'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Heredity means the inheritance of traits from one generation to the next.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Reproduction gives offspring a common basic body design, along with subtle changes in it.

scenes.animation: A generation tree builds from top to bottom, as in the textbook figure: one organism gives two in the first generation, each with one coloured dot of difference; the next generation keeps the old dot and adds a new one, so dots pile up. Label: 'variations accumulate'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Watch this tree for an asexually reproducing organism. The first generation has two individuals, slightly different because DNA copying is not perfect.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the second generation, each one passes on its difference and adds a new one. So variations accumulate over generations.

scenes.animation: Split screen: left side shows asexual offspring in a row, near-identical, labelled 'minor differences'; right side shows two parents whose DNA strands braid together, producing a varied row of offspring labelled 'greater diversity'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Is there more variation in asexual or sexual reproduction?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In asexual reproduction, the differences are very minor, caused only by small errors in DNA copying.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In sexual reproduction, DNA from two individuals combines. So it generates much greater diversity.

scenes.animation: A group of cartoon bacteria faces a heat wave; the sun icon pulses and a thermometer rises. Only the bacteria wearing tiny sun-hats survive and multiply. Label: 'environment selects variants'. Tip card slides in.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Are all variations equally useful?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. Different individuals have different kinds of advantages, depending on the environment.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For example, bacteria that can withstand heat will survive better in a heat wave.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The selection of such variants by environmental factors forms the basis for evolutionary processes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: if asked why sexual reproduction gives more variation, write that it combines DNA from two different individuals.

scenes.animation: Neo at the chalkboard as three recap points appear with ticks: '1. Heredity: traits passed on', '2. Variations accumulate; sexual > asexual', '3. Environment selects useful variants'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: heredity is the inheritance of traits, with a common body design and small variations.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: variations accumulate over generations, and sexual reproduction creates far more variation than asexual reproduction.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: variations give different survival advantages, and the environment selects the useful ones.

scenes.animation: A kitchen table heaped with pea pods. Neo sits with a notebook, sorting peas into labelled bowls and tallying marks. Zippy peeks in holding a sabzi ladle.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, why are you counting peas? Is this for tonight's sabzi?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not sabzi, science. A monk named Gregor Mendel counted pea plants like this and discovered the rules of inheritance.

scenes.animation: Two parent silhouettes each hand over a DNA bundle of equal size to a child silhouette. Then three pairs of contrasting pea traits appear as cards: 'round / wrinkled seeds', 'tall / short plants', 'violet / white flowers'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Both the father and the mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material to the child. So each child has two versions of every trait, one from each parent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mendel used garden peas with clear contrasting traits, like round or wrinkled seeds, tall or short plants, and violet or white flowers.

scenes.animation: A tall pea plant and a short pea plant stand on two pots with a '×' between them. A row of F1 plants pops up below, all tall. Label: 'F1: all tall'. Zippy scratches his head.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He crossed a pure tall plant with a pure short plant. The first generation, called F1, were all tall. None were medium height.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the short trait just vanished?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's what it looks like. Let's check the next generation.

scenes.animation: An F1 tall plant self-pollinates with a small sparkle. Four F2 plants grow: three tall and one short, which pops up with a cheeky wave. Label: 'F2: 3/4 tall, 1/4 short'. Words 'dominant' and 'recessive' stamp onto the tall and short plants.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He let the F1 plants self-pollinate. In the F2 generation, three quarters were tall and one quarter were short.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the F1 plants carried the short trait, hidden. The trait that shows is called dominant, here tallness. The hidden one is recessive, here shortness.

scenes.animation: A checkerboard builds: parents 'TT' and 'tt' give F1 'Tt'. Then a 2 by 2 grid for 'Tt × Tt' fills in with 'TT', 'Tt', 'Tt', 'tt'; three boxes turn green (tall), one turns grey (short). Ratio '3 : 1' and '1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt' appear. Tip card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now with letters. A pure tall plant is TT, and a pure short plant is tt. The F1 is Tt, and it's tall, because a single copy of T is enough for tallness.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Crossing Tt with Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt. That's three tall to one short, a three to one ratio. By letters, it's one TT, two Tt, one tt.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: a tall plant can be TT or Tt, but a short plant must be tt. Always show the checkerboard, it earns marks.

scenes.animation: Neo at the chalkboard beside a small checkerboard thumbnail as recap points appear: '1. Both parents contribute equally', '2. F1 all tall: tall is dominant', '3. F2 = 3 tall : 1 short'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: both parents contribute practically equal genetic material, so every trait has two copies.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: when pure tall and pure short plants are crossed, all F1 plants are tall, so tallness is dominant.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: self-pollinating F1 gives an F2 ratio of three tall to one short, bringing back the recessive trait.

scenes.animation: A snack counter menu board lists 'Round Yellow', 'Wrinkled Green' combos. Zippy points at the board and orders a combo that isn't listed; the shopkeeper, a talking pea pod, shrugs.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: One round green pea combo, please! Wait, that's not on the menu.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Mendel's garden, new combos did appear. Let's see how, when we track two traits at once.

scenes.animation: Two parent pea seeds appear with labels: 'Round, green: RRyy' and 'Wrinkled, yellow: rrYY', with a '×' between. A row of F1 seeds pops out, all round and yellow, labelled 'RrYy'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mendel crossed plants with round, green seeds and plants with wrinkled, yellow seeds. Round is R, and yellow is Y.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: All the F1 seeds were round and yellow. So round is dominant over wrinkled, and yellow is dominant over green.

scenes.animation: The F1 plant self-pollinates. Four gamete types slide out as tiles: 'RY', 'Ry', 'rY', 'ry'. A 4 by 4 checkerboard fills box by box with sixteen seed icons.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And when the F1 plants self-pollinate?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each F1 plant makes germ cells with four combinations: RY, Ry, rY and ry. Put them in a sixteen-box checkerboard.

scenes.animation: The sixteen boxes sort themselves into four colour-coded groups: 9 round yellow, 3 round green, 3 wrinkled yellow, 1 wrinkled green. Ratio '9 : 3 : 3 : 1' bounces up; the two new combinations sparkle with a 'NEW!' tag.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The F2 has four kinds of seeds: nine round yellow, three round green, three wrinkled yellow and one wrinkled green, out of sixteen.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Look at round green and wrinkled yellow. Neither F1 plant looked like that. These are new combinations.

scenes.animation: Two separate conveyor belts, one carrying 'seed shape' tiles and one carrying 'seed colour' tiles, move without touching each other and meet only at the end to form combinations. Label: 'inherited independently'. Tip card slides in.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So seed shape and seed colour don't travel together?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Right. New combinations mean the two traits are inherited independently of each other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mendel saw the same with tall plants and round seeds. The F2 included tall plants with wrinkled seeds, and short plants with round seeds.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: learn the 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 ratio, and write that new combinations prove independent inheritance. Also check each trait alone: twelve round to four wrinkled is still three to one.

scenes.animation: Neo at the chalkboard beside a mini 4 by 4 grid as recap points appear: '1. F1 all round yellow', '2. F2 = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1', '3. New combinations → independent inheritance'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: crossing round green with wrinkled yellow gives F1 seeds that are all round and yellow.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the F2 shows four types in the ratio nine to three to three to one.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: new combinations appear, showing that different traits are inherited independently.

scenes.animation: A giant letter 'T' stands next to a pea plant, holding a megaphone and shouting at it; the plant doesn't budge. Zippy watches, confused.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, how does the letter T make a pea plant tall? Does it just shout 'grow'?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ha! No. The T stands for a gene, and genes work through proteins. Let's see how.

scenes.animation: Zoom into a cell nucleus, where a long DNA strand unrolls like a recipe scroll. One highlighted section is labelled 'gene'; an arrow leads from it to a folded protein shape labelled 'protein'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Cellular DNA is the information source for making proteins.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A section of DNA that provides information for one protein is called the gene for that protein.

scenes.animation: Split screen of two pea plants. Left: a speedy enzyme character churns out many 'hormone' drops, and the plant grows tall. Right: a sleepy enzyme makes only a few drops, and the plant stays short. Labels: 'efficient enzyme' and 'less efficient enzyme'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Plants have hormones that can trigger growth. Plant height depends on the amount of a particular plant hormone.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The amount of hormone made depends on how efficient an enzyme is in making it. And that enzyme is a protein, made using a gene.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If the gene gives an efficient enzyme, a lot of hormone is made, and the plant is tall. If the gene is altered and the enzyme is less efficient, less hormone is made, and the plant is short.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So genes control traits by controlling proteins!

scenes.animation: A cell shows its DNA as several separate coloured rods rather than one thread, labelled 'chromosomes'. Each rod has a partner; one of each pair is tinted blue ('from father') and one pink ('from mother').

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Both parents contribute equally to the DNA of the offspring. But each gene set is not one long thread. It is present as separate, independent pieces called chromosomes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each cell has two copies of each chromosome, one from the male parent and one from the female parent.

scenes.animation: The paired chromosomes split so each germ cell receives one from every pair. A male and a female germ cell then merge, and the chromosome count on a counter returns to normal with a satisfying 'ding'. Tip card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When germ cells form, each one takes just one chromosome from each pair. When a male and a female germ cell combine, the normal number of chromosomes is restored.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This keeps the DNA of the species stable across generations.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And since each pair is sorted separately, traits can mix in new combinations!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. That explains independent inheritance. Board tip: 'a gene is a section of DNA that provides information for one protein' is a frequent one-mark answer.

scenes.animation: Neo at the chalkboard as recap points appear with small icons: '1. Gene → protein', '2. Efficient enzyme → more hormone → tall', '3. Germ cells get one chromosome of each pair'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a gene is a section of DNA that provides information for one protein.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: genes control traits through proteins, like an enzyme that decides how much growth hormone a plant makes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: germ cells carry one chromosome from each pair, so fertilisation restores the normal number.

scenes.animation: A sandy nest of cartoon reptile eggs with a thermometer stuck in the sand. Zippy holds a clipboard; as the thermometer needle moves up and down, little 'M' and 'F' tags flicker above the eggs.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, is it true that for some animals, a thermometer decides whether the baby is male or female?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In some animals, yes. The temperature at which fertilised eggs are kept decides the sex of the young ones.

scenes.animation: A cartoon snail slides across a leaf and its label flips from 'male' to 'female' with a card-flip effect. Then a human silhouette appears with a DNA icon and the label 'genetically determined'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In some animals like snails, individuals can even change sex. So sex is not always decided by genes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But in human beings, the sex of the individual is largely genetically determined.

scenes.animation: A neat chart of 23 chromosome pairs appears; 22 matched pairs glow grey, and the 23rd pair is highlighted. For the female chart it shows 'XX'; for the male chart it shows 'X' with a shorter 'Y'. Label: 'sex chromosomes'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Twenty-two pairs are matched in both males and females.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes. Women have a perfect pair, called X and X. Men have a mismatched pair: one normal-sized X and one short Y.

scenes.animation: A cross diagram builds: mother 'XX' gives only 'X' eggs; father 'XY' gives 'X' sperms and 'Y' sperms. Arrows combine them into 'XX: girl' and 'XY: boy', each tagged '50%'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So how is the sex of a child decided?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: All children get an X chromosome from their mother, because she has only X chromosomes to give.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the sex depends on what the child inherits from the father. An X from the father gives a girl, and a Y gives a boy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Since half the sperms carry X and half carry Y, the chance of a girl or a boy is equal.

scenes.animation: An old-fashioned speech bubble reading 'It's the mother's fault!' appears; Neo pops it with a pin, and the words 'Myth' and 'Science: depends on father's chromosome' appear. Tip card slides in.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So blaming a mother for having a daughter makes no sense!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: None at all. Science shows the mother always contributes an X. And both daughters and sons are equally welcome.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: draw the XX by XY cross diagram in your answer. It is the clearest way to show why the chance is fifty-fifty.

scenes.animation: Neo at the chalkboard beside a mini XX by XY cross diagram as recap points appear: '1. Some animals: temperature decides sex', '2. Humans: XX female, XY male', '3. Father's X or Y decides the child's sex'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: in some animals, the temperature of the fertilised eggs decides the sex, and snails can change sex.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: in humans, sex is genetically determined, with women having XX and men having XY.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the mother always gives an X, so the father's X or Y decides whether the child is a girl or a boy.
